1.pericope_label: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits: he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then an herald cried aloud, To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up: And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. Therefore at that time, when all the people heard the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and all kinds of musick, all the people, the nations, and the languages, fell down and worshipped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch work through the seven classes of officers with Persian etymologies, making the first the king's chief representatives and the second probably military commanders; Ellicott supposes the image was wood covered with thin plates of gold, observes that its height is out of proportion to its width so that the sixty cubits probably include the pedestal, takes the three terms of the proclamation for all nations under the empire, and notes that burning was not an unusual penalty there and that at a national festival refusal counted as treason.

Gill makes the image a shell of plate or a gilded wooden core, since the bulk would otherwise swallow a prodigious quantity of gold, lists the candidates for whom it honoured and offers motives instead — vanity, a wish to display the monarchy as an image all of gold rather than a head of gold, and a design to contradict the dream that promised his empire an end — and thinks one herald could not have carried across such a crowd, so that the singular stands for many voices about the plain in different tongues; Calvin dismisses as frivolous the guess that the statue was a charm to avert the dream, doubts the king deified himself, thinks he consecrated it to an existing god, and is sure only of the mixture of motives, since men who spend on temples say it is for God's honour and are advancing their own; on the officers he refuses the whole etymological exercise, since he does not know the derivations, the words are not Hebrew and the Jews know no more of their origin than he does, and the subtler explanations assert nothing but what is frivolous, and he says the same of the instruments; on the edict he sees what was not required, since no profession of belief was demanded and bending the knee was enough, which is why the excuse fails for anyone who bows while privately dissenting, God asking first for the worship of the mind.

Clarke suspects the sixty cubits include a high pedestal, reproduces another scholar's derivations of the official titles at length, identifies each of the musical instruments in turn and quotes a traveller's description of one as a triangle strung with twenty catguts, and notices that this is the first place in the older Scriptures where time is divided into hours, the Greeks having credited the invention to one of their own who probably had it from the Chaldeans; Wesley suggests the king was clearing himself of the suspicion that he had gone over to the Jews after praising their God, and says the proclamation was made in several languages.

Henry observes that rich as the king was he likely could not have afforded solid gold, and that the worshippers of false gods never count the cost of an image, lavishing gold out of the bag in a way that shames our stinginess toward the true God; and he takes the setting up of one more idol in a city already full of them for the standing condition of idolatry, since those who leave the one living God find what they set up so unsatisfying that they multiply gods without measure.

debates.question: Whom or what was the golden image meant to honour?

positions.position: Unrecoverable: the king himself, his father, the chief god, or a new deity are all possible, and the likelier motives are vanity and a wish to contradict the dream.
Probably an existing god rather than the king himself; the guess that it was a charm against the dream is frivolous.
A means of clearing himself of the suspicion that he had gone over to the Jews.

debates.question: How should the untranslatable titles and instruments be handled?

positions.position: Derive them: each office and instrument can be traced, and a traveller's description supplies what the words do not.
Derive them from Persian, class by class.
Refuse the exercise: the words are not Hebrew, the Jews know no more of their origin than we do, and the subtler explanations are frivolous.

outliers.claim: Notices that this is the first passage in the older Scriptures to divide time into hours, and argues that the Greek credited with inventing the division probably took it from the Chaldeans.
Presses that the edict demanded no profession of belief at all, only the bending of the knee, which is exactly why bowing while privately dissenting is no defence.

8.pericope_label: Wherefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near, and accused the Jews. They spake and said to the king Nebuchadnezzar, O king, live for ever. Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man that shall hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, shall fall down and worship the golden image: And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth, that he should be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the accusers from the astrologers, making them native subjects set against the Jewish colonists, supposes the promotion of three foreigners had long been watched with jealousy, reads the mention of their office as explaining both the king's anger at apparent ingratitude and the malice of the complaint, and turns Daniel's absence into an argument about the book itself: his later conduct puts it beyond question that he would not have joined the rite, and whatever kept him away, the silence shows that the book is not written to glorify Daniel and that an author inventing the story would have arranged a miracle to rescue him too.

Gill takes the singular verb to mean Daniel first thought of the refusal and moved it to the others, places the accusers' approach either at the palace or out on the plain with the assembly still standing, and hears contempt in the bare phrase certain Jews, which sets them down as foreigners, exiles and captives, unfit for trust and never worth the king's notice; Calvin reads the whole ceremony as a trap, since kings who despise God still arm themselves with religion to hold their subjects, and the statue was set in a public place as a test of whether the Jews would conform, the counsellors being behind it because men who were slaves by right of war had been made prefects over them — the proof lying in the speed of the accusation, since nobody discovers so quickly that a particular man has not bowed unless he was standing there to watch him; he also explains why only three are named, the charge being confined to the hard case because breaking these would carry the rest.
Clarke agrees that Daniel was probably too eminent to be touched, notes that the other Jews present went unremarked as well, and is certain he was not among the worshippers.

Henry finds it strange that the three attended at all, knowing what the assembly was for, and answers that they meant to obey as far as obedience could go and to bear their testimony where it would be seen, since it was not enough, holding office as they did, merely to refrain from bowing; on the accusers he offers two guesses, that they were of the class Daniel had eclipsed and returned evil for the good his prayers had done them, or that they wanted the offices themselves, adding that we should not find such ingratitude strange; and he notes the respectful preface and loyal compliment of the charge, as though the accusers cared for nothing but the king's honour when what they urged would have ruined him.

debates.question: Why was Daniel not accused with the other three?

positions.position: Business, or leave to withdraw, or a standing so high that nobody dared complain of him.
He was probably too eminent to be touched, and certainly was not among the worshippers.
The reason cannot be recovered, but the silence proves the book is not written to glorify Daniel, since an inventor would have given him a miracle too.
Professional grudge or plain envy of the offices the three had been given.
Jealousy of foreigners promoted over native subjects, watched for a long while.
A trap laid from the start: the counsellors advised the statue as a test of Jewish conformity, which is why the accusation followed so fast.

outliers.claim: Argues from Daniel's unexplained absence that the book cannot be fiction, since an inventor would certainly have supplied a miracle to deliver its hero along with the other three.
Hears deliberate contempt in the phrase certain Jews, which reduces the accused to foreigners and captives and implies that the king blundered in ever promoting them.

13.pericope_label: Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego. Then they brought these men before the king. Nebuchadnezzar spake and said unto them, Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, do not ye serve my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up? Now if ye be ready that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the image which I have made; well: but if ye worship not, ye shall be cast the same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace; and who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands? Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter. If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note that the three address the king by his own name in answer to his address to them, and take the word for able in an ethical sense, the power as bounded by God's own holiness rather than bare omnipotence, which they say the three would never have called into question before a heathen king; they deny expressly that the answer shows audacity, or superstitious expectation of a wonder, or fanaticism, finding in it only faith and submission. Ellicott takes the same address as directing attention to the antithesis between the king's demand and their reply, observes that the distance between king and subject simply closes where duty to God collides with a royal edict, gives the opening phrase as we have no need, and would drop the word so from the conditional so that it reads: if our God is able to deliver us, he will do so, and if he does not, we still will not serve your gods — on which reading there is not the slightest ground for supposing they expected a miracle, since they never questioned the power and simply did not know the will.

Gill hears the reply as mild and unaffronting, neither insulting the king's gods nor descending to servile fear or flattery, and takes the men as resigned should God not think fit to exert a power they are well assured he has; Calvin marks what the constancy cost, since with that death set immediately before them they did not swerve, valuing God's glory above their lives and above a hundred lives had they possessed them, sums the opening phrase as a declaration that the matter is settled, and makes their firmness rest on two supports, a settled persuasion that their lives were in God's keeping and would be given back if that were useful, and a readiness to die outright if he preferred that sacrifice — turning it on the reader, since most men fall away for want of confidence in the first, and scarcely one in a hundred holds it fixed in the heart.

Clarke expands the opening phrase into we need not put thee to further trouble, our minds are made up and our answer is ready, and calls this as honest as it was decisive; on the conditional he takes the opposite line from Ellicott, holding that though the three are equally determined if no rescue comes they are satisfied that in some way God will deliver them out of the king's hand, since his power cannot reach them in the kingdom they would ascend to from his furnace; and he draws the political rule, that one renders to the sovereign what is his, but where the sovereign claims what belongs to God his authority is to be resisted; Wesley makes the phrase plainer still, that debating is useless since the king is resolved to have his will and they are resolved otherwise, says it was all one to them which way God chose to honour himself, and puts the whole in a line — that God will deliver either from death or in death.

debates.question: Did the three expect to be delivered?

positions.position: No: there is not the slightest ground for supposing they expected a miracle; they never questioned the power and did not know the will.
Neither audacity nor superstitious expectation nor fanaticism, but faith and humble submission; the word for able is bounded by God's holiness, not bare omnipotence.
Yes, in a manner: equally determined if no rescue came, but satisfied that in some way God would deliver them out of the king's hand.
It was all one to them which way God chose to honour himself, since he would deliver either from death or in death.

debates.question: What does the opening phrase of the reply mean?

positions.position: We have no need — it is needless to give any reply.
We need not put thee to further trouble; our minds are made up and our answer ready.
A declaration that the matter is settled.

outliers.claim: Draws a political rule out of the refusal, that the sovereign is to be rendered what is his, but where he claims what belongs to God his authority is to be resisted.
Turns the men's two supports on the reader, since most fall away for want of confidence that their lives are in God's keeping, and scarcely one in a hundred holds that fixed in the heart.

19.pericope_label: Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated. And he commanded the most mighty men that were in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. Therefore because the king’s commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego. And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, fell down bound into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the mechanics of the furnace, which must have had a mouth above through which victims were thrown, a task ordinarily safe but not at this heat, and say the death of the executioners is recorded to measure the miracle; on the clothing they deny the garments are hose and match the word to a Semitic term for a tunic. Ellicott doubts that the sevenfold heating is a round number and offers the possibility that the Babylonians reckoned seven demons the most formidable of the infernal powers, so the figure may point to them, the punishment having a religious character and the overheating a religious act; he corrects the phrase to than it was fitting, notes that the impropriety of the heating is what killed the executioners, supposes the strong men were chosen as likeliest to endure the heat with the army evidently present, orders the garments as an under-garment, a tunic spread over it and a cloak probably reserved for state occasions, and sets the death of those who carried out the sentence against the survival of those sentenced.

Gill says the king was nettled to find his threats had made no impression, takes the executioners for the most famous in the army for courage and strength, allows that an Arabic usage would make the first garment breeches, and notes that the old versions insert sixty-seven verses of a song absent from the Hebrew; Calvin notes that at first sight God appears to desert his servants, no help showing itself, and that their courage never depended on expecting any, and distinguishes the two halves of the wonder, the outer edge of the fire consuming strong men by merely playing about them while those in its heart walked unharmed.

Clarke marvels at a man who had watched his authority overturned before and would try his strength again, takes seven for as hot as the furnace could be made, reads the executioners as generals or chief officers since mere strength was not what the task required, observes that one of the garment-words occurs nowhere else in the older Scriptures and cites Herodotus for a Babylonian dress of linen and woollen tunics under a short white cloak with a turban, rendering the list so that the outermost garments are named — which is why the later verse about their being unaltered tells — and adds that the join between this verse and the next is visibly broken where the old versions insert the song; Wesley asks what the king can have been thinking, whether that three bound men would resist, or that their God would shield them, or that the strongest soldiers could prevail if he did, and answers that God meant to show his power when the king did his worst, adding that a flame which killed the executioners outside could have killed the bound men more easily, before they landed.

Henry expects the opposite reaction from a man who had owned so much of the true God, observes that passions indulged grow more violent and show in the face, and that a prince who traded the majesty of the throne for the look of a wild bull in a net would have blushed to see himself in a glass; he also sees the cruelty in the direction of the change, since rank might have earned mitigation and got the opposite.

debates.question: Why were the mightiest men in the army chosen to do it?

positions.position: For courage and bodily strength, being the most famous in the army.
As likeliest to endure the heat, the army being evidently present.
They were generals or chief officers, since mere strength was not what the task required.

debates.question: What does the sevenfold heating signify?

positions.position: Simply as hot as the furnace could be made, seven expressing intensity.
Possibly the seven demons the Babylonians reckoned most formidable, the overheating being itself a religious act.
An aggravation of the sentence where rank might have earned mitigation.

outliers.claim: Turns the king's rage into a study of temper, since indulged passions show in the face and a prince who exchanges the majesty of the throne for the look of a wild bull in a net would blush to see himself in a glass.
Notes that the join between this verse and the next is visibly broken, which is where the old versions insert a song of sixty-seven verses absent from the Hebrew.

24.pericope_label: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonied, and rose up in haste, and spake, and said unto his counsellors, Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire? They answered and said unto the king, True, O king. He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace, and spake, and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, ye servants of the most high God, come forth, and come hither. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, came forth of the midst of the fire. And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king’s counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them. Then Nebuchadnezzar spake, and said, Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants that trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God. Therefore I make a decree, That every people, nation, and language, which speak any thing amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, shall be cut in pieces, and their houses shall be made a dunghill: because there is no other God that can deliver after this sort. Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed–nego, in the province of Babylon.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the closing phrase as after this sort rather than this God, holding that a visible deity suited the heathen mind better than an invisible one, so the decree fixes on the manner of deliverance rather than on the person delivering. Ellicott places the king at an opening in the furnace wall from which he could watch, holds the middle ground on the fourth figure by noting that the words come from a heathen who calls the same person an angel four verses later and who probably imagined him standing to the God of Israel as he himself stood to his own god, grants that the early fathers read the place of Christ but says that beyond this we have no means of knowing and must be content that the presence which went with Israel in the wilderness watched over them in Babylon, and takes the promotion as a reinstatement to the offices they had held.

Gill divides the king's astonishment between the death of his own men and a panic sent directly upon him, notices exactly what the king reports, four men loose and walking separately where three had gone in tied, and turns the furnace into a figure of affliction in which men are loosed from the hold of sin even while bound in every other sense; on the confession he grants the force of conviction but denies a thorough conversion, since the king did not give up his own gods. Calvin reads the question to the counsellors as arranged, God meaning the admission to come from the men who had engineered the affair so that the rescue could not be laid to any earthly cause, rests the weight of the inspection on the last item, that not even the smell of fire had passed on them, values the witnesses because they were the enemies, denies the confession is repentance since repentance consists not in one or two acts but in perseverance, finds the tell-tale in the pronoun because the king never calls that God his own, allows the decree pious in itself while denying its author any credit, and observes that the whole province had seen these men thrown into a furnace and restored to office, so the story travelled as if three heralds had been sent through the country.

Clarke calls the received rendering of the fourth figure a most improper translation, asks what notion an idolatrous king could have of Christ, and insists the phrase means a son of the gods, a divine being or angel, which is precisely what the king calls the figure a few verses later; he supplies the sceptical parallel to the escape and disposes of it, since heathen priests were said to walk on hot coals unhurt and a Latin poet describes it, but another writer explains that they oiled their feet first, whereas the officers here knew no such trick would answer; he calls the confession a noble testimony from a heathen and asks what produced it, since had the three been time-servers the true God's name would never have been heard in Babylon; and he notes that the edict does not require anyone to worship the God of Israel, only to speak of him with reverence. Wesley takes the older view, that the Angel of the covenant did sometimes appear before the incarnation, and draws from it that those who suffer for Christ have his presence with them in the furnace.

Henry rests the proof of the miracle on the inspection, observing that the examination was made by princes who could not be suspected of partiality, and takes the confession at its word as evidence that God can extort acknowledgements of his blessedness from men ready to curse him.

debates.question: Who was the fourth figure in the furnace?

positions.position: A divine being or angel; the received rendering is an improper translation, since an idolatrous king could have no notion of Christ.
The Angel of the covenant, who did sometimes appear before the incarnation.
Unknowable beyond the heathen speaker's own meaning; the fathers read it of Christ, but the words are a Babylonian's and he calls the same person an angel four verses later.

debates.question: Was the king's confession a conversion?

positions.position: Yes in substance, a noble testimony from a heathen, and evidence that God extorts acknowledgements from men ready to curse him.
No; conviction without conversion, since he did not give up his own gods and never calls that God his own, and repentance consists in perseverance rather than in one or two acts.

outliers.claim: Meets the fire-walking parallel head on, since a Latin poet describes priests treading hot coals unhurt, but another writer explains that they oiled their feet beforehand, a trick the officers at the furnace knew would not answer.
Reads the decree's closing phrase as after this sort rather than this God, a visible manner of deliverance suiting the heathen mind better than an invisible deity.
